column2: These are the most wanted chips on Earth. And until last week, one man stood behind them: Nvidia's Jensen Huang.
The AI boom runs on Nvidia's chips. By early November, the company was worth about four and a half trillion dollars.
That makes the chips political. Washington decides which ones China can buy. Last December, it let Nvidia sell a far stronger one.
Then The New York Times reported that U.S. officials believe Alice Huang, a businesswoman close to Jensen, is a Chinese intelligence asset.
She's no relation. No proof has been made public, and China calls it a smear. But one question stuck: how close were they?
On November eighth, Huang answered in a letter to his staff. I was unfaithful to my wife, he wrote. There is no excuse for what I did.
The board said it saw no sign that secrets were compromised. But the threads kept pulling. Shares fell. Congress wanted answers. And new reports surfaced of relationships with Nvidia employees.
Four days after his letter, Huang resigned as chief executive. The company's finance chief, Colette Kress, is now running Nvidia for the time being.

More than a hundred and seventy thousand people have signed a letter asking for him back. The board reportedly isn't considering it. And officials still haven't said whether Alice Huang was really a spy.
The chips are still the most wanted on Earth. The man who built the company around them just isn't holding them anymore.
